title: James V. DiIorio Obituary | Ironside Funeral Home | Oneida, NY - Tribute Archive
content: 2 Trees, Flowers, or Condolences have been sent in support of James’s family — View on Tribute Wall 2 Trees, Flowers, or Condolences have been sent in support of James’s family — View on Tribute Wall James V. “Jim” DiIorio, 69, of Sylvan Beach, passed away on Wednesday, August 19, 2026, at his home under the care of Hospice and Palliative Care. Jim was born on March 4, 1957, in Cortland, the son of Americo and Elvira (Scarano) DiIorio.  Jim was a 1975 graduate of Cortland High School. He earned his bachelor's degree from SUNY Cortland and earned his master’s degree from SUNY Oswego. On February 16, 2013, Jim was united in marriage to Tina L. Deeley. Jim dedicated twenty-eight years of his professional life to Madison-Oneida BOCES, where he served as a graphic design instructor. Through his creativity, patience, and knowledge of the trade, he helped educate and inspire countless students, sharing with them not only the technical skills of graphic design, but also the importance of pride in their work. He retired in 2015 after a rewarding career in education. Away from the classroom, Jim had a wide variety of interests and enjoyed staying involved in his community. He was a member of the Sons of the American Legion Post 1153 and was especially proud of the friendships and camaraderie he found there. Athletics were also an important part of Jim’s life. For 22 years, he coached varsity wrestling at Oneida High School, where he mentored generations of student-athletes. His influence extended well beyond wins and losses, as he encouraged his wrestlers to work hard, remain disciplined, and always give their best. Jim was also an avid sports fan, faithfully cheering on the Dallas Cowboys and the New York Yankees. Jim enjoyed spending time on the golf course and was a longtime member of a golf league at Old Erie Golf Club. He also loved the freedom of the open road and was often found riding his Harley-Davidson whenever the weather allowed. Jim was also well known for his culinary talents, particularly his famous white chili. A fixture at the Maynard Pines White Chili competition, Jim proudly earned numerous medals over the years and enjoyed the good-natured competition almost as much as sharing his award-winning creation with others. Surviving besides his loving wife, Tina; are his stepchildren, Mycale (Nick) Crisafi of Clay, and Matt Harp of Sherrill; his granddaughter, Laikyn Harp; his brothers and sisters-in-law, Paul (Darlene) Deeley of Zephyr Hills, FL, Sherry Warren of Brantingham, Lisa Hammon, of Rome, and Tabatha Hoffner, of Rome; and many nieces and nephews. Jim was predeceased by his brother, Raymon DiIorio on November 22, 2018. Jim’s family wishes to express their gratitude to his special caregivers and Tina’s lifesavers, Sarah Congden, Sherry Warren, Lisa Clark, and Janelle Swafford, for the kindness and compassion shown to him. Funeral services will be held on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, at 12:30 PM at St. Mary of the Lake Church, Verona Beach, where the Rev. Christopher J. Ballard will officiate. Interment will take place in McConnellsville Cemetery. Family and friends are invited and may call prior to his Funeral Mass from 10:00 AM to 12:00 PM at the Ironside Family Funeral Homes, Inc., 342 Main St., Oneida. Memorial contributions may be made in Jim’s memory to Alzheimer's Association of CNY, 5015 Campuswood Dr Ste 102, East Syracuse, NY, 13057. To send flowers to the family or plant a tree in memory of James, please visit our floral store. title: Tony V’s Garage Closed Permanently - My Everett News
content:
A month ago a sign on Tony V’s Garage said it was closed for “summer break.” People were worried it might have closed down. No posts had been made on Facebook since early April. Bands and patrons started reminiscing good times they had at the music venue. That fear has now been realized as the Tony V’s Instagram shared a picture of the for lease sign: “Tony V’s Garage has come to end. Thank you for 17 wonderful years.” Tony V’s opened up in 2008 and was owned and operated by Tony Verhey. Before Tony V’s Garage, the live music and bar was Jimmy Z’s. Jimmy Z’s operated for about 25 years as a local hub for regional and national rock, punk, and alternative acts in Everett. Tony V’s Garage was known for the alternative, hard-rock, and metal bands. In addition to live music, some people love going there for burgers and beers. In 2016, Tony expanded the bar by moving into the space next door at 1716 Hewitt Ave. The venue is now 7,500 square feet. Hopefully a new live music venue will take its place. title: Peru selects AN/ALQ-254(V)1 Viper Shield electronic warfare system for its F-16 Block 70 fleet - Aviacionline
content: L3Harris Technologies was selected by the Government of Peru to provide the AN/ALQ-254(V)1 Viper Shield electronic warfare system for the F-16 Block 70s that will join the Peruvian Air Force (FAP). The decision specifically confirms the solution chosen for the 24 Peruvian fighters, after the US approval of September 2025 included the Viper Shield or an equivalent system within the acquisition package. The system will be integrated into the new F-16s alongside the AN/APG-83 AESA radar, giving the aircraft a sensor and electronic self-protection architecture designed to operate against modern threats. The Viper Shield was developed by L3Harris in partnership with Lockheed Martin and the United States Air Force specifically for the most advanced F-16 models. The suite uses a fully digital, software-defined architecture, featuring a Digital Radar Warning Receiver (DRWR) and electronic countermeasure capabilities based on Digital Radio Frequency Memory (DRFM). Operationally, the system detects and processes electromagnetic signals associated with threats, giving the pilot the information needed to identify the radar environment and generate electronic responses designed to increase the aircraft's survivability. One of its most important aspects is its integration with the AN/APG-83 AESA radar. The combination allows sensors and electronic warfare systems to operate on a common mission architecture, improving the pilot's situational awareness in an increasingly complex electromagnetic environment. The open, software-defined architecture also allows new capabilities to be incorporated as threats evolve, reducing the need to physically replace the entire system to introduce future upgrades. The selection of the Viper Shield is particularly significant given the expected service life of Peru's new fighters. The system was designed to reduce size, weight and the number of components compared with previous generations, while also easing maintenance through line-replaceable units. Its architecture also allows software updates and new electronic warfare applications to be introduced during the aircraft's operational life. The matter is especially relevant for a fleet intended to progressively replace the MiG-29 and Mirage 2000, whose sustainment and modernization have become one of the main challenges of Peruvian combat aviation. L3Harris reported that eight countries have already selected the Viper Shield and that the company is ramping up production toward a target of 233 systems. That figure adds an extra dimension to the Peruvian decision. The system is not only part of the F-16 Block 70 configuration, but is also moving toward an international user base sharing a common electronic warfare architecture. In that sense, the Viper Shield will be one of the pieces that will determine how long the Peruvian F-16 Block 70 can maintain its regional technological edge: not only because of the capabilities it brings at delivery, but also because of its ability to evolve alongside the electromagnetic environment in which it will have to operate.

title: Colts QB Daniel Jones a standout performer in joint practice v. Falcons - Yahoo Sports
content: Quarterback Daniel Jones was a standout performer for the Indianapolis Colts in the team's first joint practice with the Atlanta Falcons. Kevin Bowen of 107.5 The Fan called it a "flawless afternoon." ESPN's Stephen Holder posted on X that Jones was "on fire" for most of the day. By Bowen's unofficial count, he had Jones going 14-for-14 on the day against the Atlanta secondary, and that was without Alec Pierce still and Tyler Warren exiting the game. Bowen notes that Ashton Dulin and Seth McGowan had particularly good days in the passing game. "It wasn't anything overly flashy from Jones," wrote Bowen. "He did have one tipped pass, fortunately fall into the hands of Josh Downs for a nice gain. But after a few practices of some rockier moments, Jones and the passing offense was much, much better." The Indy Star's Joel Erickson called it a "rare perfect performance in a lengthy training-camp setting." As is going to be the case for any player or position group through training camp, there will be ups and downs. But by all accounts, Jones has experienced a lot more ups this summer. His ability to hit the ground running during the regular season will be vital, with the Colts beginning the year with a difficult stretch. The team re-signed Jones to a two-year, $88 million deal this offseason, hoping that he and the offense as a whole can regain their early 2025 season form. Through 10 games, Jones was one of the more productive quarterbacks in football, while the offense was off to a red-hot start. title: The Inner Circle acknowledges V. Ray Cordry, Jr., DO as a 2026 Preferred Psychiatrist - Yahoo Finance Singapore
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results HENNESSY, Okla., Aug. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Prominently featured in The Inner Circle, V. Ray Cordry, Jr., DO is acknowledged as a 2026 Preferred Psychiatrist for his contributions to Behavioral Health and Psychiatric Care. Dr. V. Ray Cordry, Jr., DO, has built a distinguished career in psychiatry marked by decades of clinical excellence, education, and compassionate patient care. As a psychiatrist at Red Rock Behavioral Health Services, he provides treatment for adults facing complex psychiatric conditions, including bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, post traumatic stress disorder, and trauma related to domestic violence. In his current role, Dr. Cordry oversees eight nurse practitioners while also teaching medical students, reflecting his strong commitment to mentorship and the advancement of psychiatric education. He is widely respected for his diagnostic precision and deep expertise in psychopharmacology, particularly in the long term management of chronic psychiatric illness. Dr. Cordry began his professional journey as a high school science teacher before pursuing medicine, a foundation that continues to influence his passion for education. He earned a Bachelor of Science in secondary science education from Phillips University and later received his Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine from the Kansas City College of Osteopathic Medicine. He completed a psychiatry residency at the University of Kansas School of Medicine followed by a child psychiatry fellowship at Oklahoma University Health Sciences Center. Board certified in general psychiatry by the American Osteopathic Board of Neurology and Psychiatry, Dr. Cordry maintains active affiliations with the American Osteopathic Association, the American Psychiatric Association, and the Oklahoma Psychiatric Association. Over the course of his career, he has contributed meaningfully to both patient care and clinical training, shaping the next generation of mental health professionals. Among his early career highlights, Dr. Cordry worked with the Kansas City Chiefs as a medical student and accompanied the team to the Pro Bowl in 1972 as part of his clinical training experience. Throughout his life, he has credited mentors James Turrentine, DO, and Neil Roach, MD, for their lasting influence on his development as a physician. Outside of medicine, Dr. Cordry enjoys gardening and values time spent with his family. He has been married to Marcia Cordry, RN, for 36 years and is the proud father of four and grandfather of four. Looking ahead, Dr. Cordry plans to devote more time to teaching and lecturing, continuing to share his knowledge and experience with future clinicians while remaining dedicated to the field of psychiatry. title: Steve V. Vagner - Ozark Radio News
content: Steve was born on August 5, 1959, to William “Bill” and Glenna Wagner. He was a lifelong resident of the Willow Springs area and graduated from Willow Springs High school in 1978. Steve worked a variety of jobs before starting his career with Walmart in 1985. He remained with Walmart until his retirement in 2020. In 1999, Steve married the love of his life, Kathy, who was by his side throughout their life together. Their love and companionship were a special part of Steve’s life. Together they built a life filled with love, laughter, family, and countless memories. Their bond was a beautiful example of true love and devotion. A love that will continue to live on in the hearts of their family and all who knew them. Steve enjoyed the simple things in life. He loved deer hunting, riding four-wheelers, farming, and raising beef cattle. He also enjoyed good food, especially chocolate and Mtn Dew. Steve was known for his sense of humor and his ability to joke around with just about everyone he met. His laughter, personality, and friendship will be deeply missed by all who knew him. Steve’s faithful cat, Baby “21 years” was by his side through many years of love and companionship. She brought him joy, comfort, and unconditional love. Steve was preceded in death by his parents, William “Bill” and Glenna Wagner; his brother, Ted; sister-in-law, Cindy Wagner; and nephew, Travis. Steve is survived by his beloved wife, Kathy; his two sons, Mike (Marisa) Kelley and Timothy (Jenny) Starbuck. His grandchildren: Bayler, Camden, Brendan Kelley, Timothy, Steven, April, Lara, Landon, and Krystal Starbuck. His brother, Fred Wagner; three nieces, one nephew, and dear friends who loved him and will miss him dearly. Steve leaves behind a lifetime of memories for his family and friends. Steve lived a good life. One built on hard work, kindness, and love. He was a devoted husband, a proud father, a loving grandfather, and a true friend. He will be remembered for the way he could light up a room with his smile, the way he always had time for others, and the way he loved his family more than anything. Our hearts are heavy with his loss. His legacy of love, strength, and laughter will live on in all of us.

title: Whistleblower Arturo Béjar leads testimony in landmark trial against Meta - NPR
content:
Former Meta engineer Arturo Bejar leaves the Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building & United States Courthouse as Meta is on trial over social media addiction in Oakland, California, on August 19, 2026.
                
                    
                    KARL MONDON/AFP via Getty Images
                    
                
hide caption Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR Meta was infused with a culture in which employees obsessed over user numbers and consistently pushed safety to the side, according to Arturo Béjar, a former employee turned whistleblower, who testified today in the landmark child safety trial against the social media company. Only one man had the ability to change that, Béjar said: CEO Mark Zuckerberg. But he didn't. "At the end of the day, it was the company culture that Mark had created that made it so that it was practically impossible to deliver features that addressed the wellbeing and safety issues that we've been talking about," he said. Béjar is a linchpin witness for a consortium of states led by California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that sued Meta, alleging violations of consumer and child data protection laws, and that the company lied to the public about risks its platforms posed. The attorneys for the states say Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to hook young users and to keep them on site longer thanks to features such as infinite scrolling and the "like" button. Meta has denied the allegations. In his opening statement on Tuesday, attorney Paul Schmidt argued that the company was sensitive to the risks to teens, sought to address them and did not deceive the public about them. The state attorneys have not yet said if they will call Zuckerberg as a witness. Testifying in federal court in Oakland, California, for a second day on Wednesday, Béjar, who worked on safety issues at Meta for eight years, said he interacted with Zuckerberg dozens of times, and charged that Zuckerberg was not telling the truth when he made public denials that the company put profits over safety. In particular, Béjar addressed a widely-shared Facebook post Zuckerberg made in 2021 after another whistleblower, Frances Haugen, shared internal documents with The Wall Street Journal that highlighted risks to the mental health of teens. In the post, Zuckerberg said it's "just not true" that Meta prioritizes profit over safety and wellbeing. "Based on my experience at Meta, that is not an accurate statement," Béjar said. On the stand, Béjar noted that he'd seen several internal Meta studies that highlighted risks for teens on Facebook and Instagram. The studies surveyed users, including teenagers, about their experiences with harmful content on the platforms and negative feelings associated with them. But he said efforts to introduce or change features to effectively address those risks were difficult to implement. Instead, Béjar testified, at almost every turn the company chose policies that boosted usership and revenue over safety. Safety was "not a meaningful priority," he said. Béjar worked at Facebook from 2009 to 2015, largely focusing on cyberbullying. He returned to the company from 2019 to 2021 as a consultant to work on Instagram's wellbeing team. He said one of the reasons for his return was seeing how his daughter was treated as a teen on Instagram. This is not the first time Béjar has spoken out against his former employer. In 2023, he testified before a Senate committee alleging that Meta pushed content to teens that promoted bullying, drug abuse, eating disorders and self-harm. He also gave an extensive interview to The Wall Street Journal that year, describing his efforts to raise his concerns with his employer. The current case, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, is a high-stakes test of efforts to hold Meta accountable, not for the content on its platforms, but for the features it built into its platforms. The states allege they were designed to encourage compulsive use, and that the company stood to financially benefit from keeping young users on site, because it makes its money through advertising. The more users scroll — and the better-targeted ads they see — the more Meta stands to profit. It is one of thousands of lawsuits against social media companies alleging that their platforms are addictive and have fueled youth mental health problems. On cross examination, Meta attorney Brian Stekloff asked Béjar about the quality of the people he worked with at Meta and whether or not he had "solved" any of the safety risks he had worked on, in an apparent effort to highlight the complexity and difficulty of these challenges. Béjar said the teams he worked with were full of qualified people whom he respected, and that none of the risk issues had been solved. He called features like video autoplay, "like" counters and infinite scroll "inherently unsafe for teenagers." And when it came to safety features Meta has introduced to try to minimize some of the risks, Béjar said they were "designed to fail." Features like Instagram's "quiet mode," which can mute push notifications, are ineffective because they are optional settings rather than defaults, he said. "Most people will not turn the setting on," he said. "It's like you have to turn on the air bag every time you get into the car." title: Thanks to Roe v. Wade, the park is missing many children - National Right to Life Committee
content: Executive Director, Pennsylvania Pro-Life Federation I decided to enjoy a breezy August day by visiting an amusement park in Pennsylvania. Throngs of families crowded into this fanciful land of roller coasters, games of chance, and high-powered swings. As I made my way to the front entrance, it occurred to me that children were missing–the children lost to abortion. They will never know the feel of cotton candy or the glow of a carousel. They will never know the simple pleasure of a day out with the family. They will never know the beauty of sun rays shining down on a boardwalk. Those who came to the park are largely the survivors. I hazard a guess that most of the guests were born after the 1973 U.S. Supreme Court decision Roe v. Wade, which brought about the abortion nightmare. I wonder how many of them think about abortion and, if they do, do they wonder how they escaped this cruelty of our age? Life should be celebrated. Children should be able to enjoy a day at the amusement park before classes begin. But, from time to time, it is good to reflect on the impact abortion has had on every facet of life in America. That includes the parks and playgrounds that are not as full as they should be, because children never got a chance at life. title: DOWN Announce ‘Volume V’ For November, Premiere “Blood Oath” Video - themosh.net
content: NOLA sludge metal supergroup DOWN have finally announced the release of their long-awaited new album, ‘Volume V’, which is now slated to arrive on November 20th via Nuclear Blast. The 10-track effort marks the band’s first proper full-length collection of new material since 2014. DOWN co-produced the record with Eddie Mapp, whose credits include Black Label Society and Stone Temple Pilots. Dave Fortman (Mudvayne, Slipknot) handled the mixing, with Maor Appelbaum (Faith No More, Halford) overseeing mastering. The album will also feature a notable guest appearance from Mercyful Fate frontman King Diamond, who contributes vocals to the track “Merciful Fate.” His wife also makes a guest appearance on the song. Another track, “Ozz,” appears to serve as a tribute to the late Ozzy Osbourne. title: Tweakadelic: second home tax, Lower Verzuh, library v. CB South - The Crested Butte News
content: Three recent local political moves this week came as no surprise, but they all provided reasons to possibly tweak us all. They did me. One will go to the voters, another to the bureaucratic process and the third apparently to court. It was a tweakadelic week in the local public realm. The Crested Butte town council on Monday not surprisingly voted 5-2 to put a second home tax on the November ballot. If approved by voters, the tax will hit second homeowners with houses in the town limits, and the amount will be based on the size of their house. I’ll go out on a limb and predict most, but not all, second homeowners will be able to easily pay the annual tax that will range from $1,400 to $3,400. But I’ll disagree with the mayor who is leading this charge and argue there were a few good reasons to not put that idea on this year’s ballot. An initial outcry from voting citizens after the idea of the second home tax was floated suggested the better way would be to dig deep into the town budget, both short-term and long-range to find cost savings and other potential revenue sources. To a person, the seven town councilmembers heartily embraced the petitioner’s idea of a citizen’s budget advisory committee. Town will solicit applications for those interested in such a position immediately and be appointing some folks at the next council meeting on September 8. Look, I think Crested Butte and probably every government entity is looking at a horizon with financial red flags given rising costs for things like asphalt for roads, maintenance for older infrastructure and construction for new projects — the things governments do. But Crested Butte isn’t going to go bankrupt next year. Over the years, it has creatively set itself up to avoid financial disaster. The town has millions of dollars in reserves. That’s not Mark Walter money, but it is still millions. There is more than $7 million in “unassigned fund reserves” in the Crested Butte General Fund. Almost $8 million in reserves is stacked up in other town funds but those are more limited. For example, $2.7 million is in the open space fund and $3.8 million in the capital fund. Those dollars are committed to specific areas of town but not allocated specifically to any particular project. Given that deep eight-figure savings account, taking the time to let the citizens committee determine what they might find and recommend, along with exploring other out-of-the-box ideas like a sales tax premium that seemed brushed aside as being too out-of-the-box, makes sense. Honestly, I don’t think there’s a lot of fat in the town budget but while not a numbers guy, I could see places to trim and things to adjust. It’s not just about revenue. The initial vacant home tax conversation certainly got the community and a core of financial-oriented citizens engaged. So why not let them do the work that the council just enthusiastically encouraged before an election is finished, not after, as this one will be. Give voters all the new and interesting information before they cast a ballot. One of my initial tweaks with this tax proposal that was reinforced this week is that many councilmembers chant the mantra that Crested Butte is different from other resort towns. It is. And part of the difference is a crusty attitude of acceptance and parity among the three legs of the economic stool (locals, tourists, second homeowners). Most local second homeowners chose CB because they love, appreciate and respect the community and our sometimes-weird mountain town culture. Most have fallen into the CB dream and see it as a real community that accepts them as people and not as a piggy bank. Putting this on the ballot challenges that part of the unwritten contract we all appreciate. I’m sure I’ll write more about all this as we move closer to the election. But as one councilmember on Monday used the metaphor of the Townie Takeover as a reason this tax deepens community, to me it looks like the council is sending the message that second homeowners can maybe (and maybe not) watch the bikes circle the Third and Elk intersection but they can’t join in unless they pay extra. That doesn’t seem right. Another no surprise political decision this week was another split vote, this time with the county commissioners. There are some really good and interesting elements in the Lacy-Dow subdivision proposal for the Lower Verzuh Ranch, but who will argue that if approved, it won’t have a major impact on the look, feel and population of the North Valley? By voting to send it through to the Preliminary Plan phase, county commissioners Liz Smith and Jonathan Houck did not guarantee any approved development. There are a lot of serious issues to work out and that is expected to take up to a year, which is months before the projected end of the corridor plan. To me, the bigger picture is what that decision does to the legitimacy of the Corridor Plan running from Gunnison to Mt. Crested Butte. This is one of a few big parcels of developable land left in the North Valley and to push it on its way without taking the time to consider the big picture corridor first, is a questionable move. While there are certain legal timelines in place for the bureaucratic process once an application is accepted, the development team did say the county should take the time it needs to work out its thought process and consider ramifications. Okay then. Take them up on the generous offer and say we as a community will first look at how we want the North Valley to grow and thanks for giving us a glimpse at what could be coming down the train tracks. It can definitely shape how much of a big city or small town we want to be as a community. Isn’t that the crux points the community should determine before pushing new major developments forward on the momentum track? Again, there are some good things in this Lower Verzuh proposal, and it could all still go through, or be rejected, but having the corridor plan in place first makes the most common sense. Commissioner Laura Pucket Daniels fought Tuesday against moving it along, not so much because of the corridor plan timing per se, but she indicated she didn’t find the application compatible with the area’s character, felt the density was too much, and impacts did not have mitigation measures identified. In other words, issues associated with a corridor plan. And finally, to the courts we go…or at least the Crested Butte South Property Owner’s Association and the Gunnison County Library District go…again. I’ve told people it seems to me this is a scuffle of personalities over policies. Of course, both sides claim they have policy on their side. Both sides claim they want the library built. Both sides say the three-story apartment complex isn’t on the horizon in the near future. Both sides claim they are simply following the rules. The on again, off again maneuvering would be almost silly chest measuring if it wasn’t getting so expensive. Both sides are using pricey Front Range lawyers. The amount of taxpayer dollars going to attorneys instead of books is now into the six figures. That tweaks me. And frankly, it should tweak you. Looking at where this kerfuffle is, and it is scheduled for a long day in district court on August 26, could everyone perhaps put aside personality and the past animosity, find a neutral mediator and spend a few hours listening? Then compromising? And then saving a ton of money and providing a good community amenity in a main population center? Aside from the housing element hanging out there, does anyone expect major pitfalls with the library building? Doubt it. But my guess is it’ll all be left up to the judge — and you never know which way that goes — except that it won’t be cheap. Anyway, I really do appreciate all of our public officials and our public processes. I genuinely like every single person involved in the three situations I just mentioned — but man, it can all be so tweakadelic sometimes. And this was one of those weeks. At least three times in the last few weeks, I’ve had the “opportunity” to sit …

title: V’s ‘Unmistakable Style’ and ‘Artistic Vision’ Helped Him Land New Champion Campaign - Rolling Stone

ARMY have long known that BTS’ V was a champ, whether he was pouring his heart out on his solo album, serving his country in the military, or pushing the limits in the gym. But now, Kim Taehyung makes it official with a new partnership with Champion, the iconic American athletic and sportswear brand. V stars as the face of the brand’s “True Champion” campaign, which celebrates “the people shaping today’s culture through their originality, perspective and enduring impact,” per a release. The singer is seen posing for a series of photographs showing off Champion’s signature sweats while debuting some new streetwear-inspired looks for the brand as well. Though the campaign images were released Aug. 10, the pieces V was wearing weren’t available to purchase online until now. Some of the pieces are only available in Korea, China or Japan, extending V’s reach as Champion’s global ambassador. However, we’ve rounded up some of the items that are available to purchase here in the U.S. This cotton blend sweatshirt features collegiate-inspired styling and a unique snap neck closure that can either be kept open like a polo collar or buttoned up for a mockneck look. A “Champion” script applique with raw edge is splashed across the chest, with an embroidered “C” patch on the left sleeve. V sports this long sleeve rugby-style top in a “tiger lily” colorway. We like the contrast-color polo collar and ribbed trim. There is an embroidered Champion script patch at the chest and a workwear label on the corner, just above the hem. Three other colors are available in sizes small to 2XL. Part of Champion’s “reverse weave” collection, which features heavyweight sweats with a worn-in look and feel, this hoodie features a contrast color drawstring, large front pouch pockets and a subtle “C” logo patch on the sleeve.This one is available in a classic fit, though you can size up if you want that trendy, oversized look. V tops off his look in this photo with a corduroy baseball cap that features both the Champion script logo and capital “C” logo embroidered on the front.The classic hat features a five-panel construction with a relaxed, “dad hat”-style fit. The back is adjustable.V paired the hat with a black Champion script sweatshirt (you can find a similar version for just $23 here). The singer’s Champion varsity jacket seen at right is currently only available in Asia, but you can find his baggy sweatpants online through Farfetch. The cotton sweats feature an elastic waistband, open hem, and the iconic C logo at the left hip.You can also find similar relaxed-fit sweatpants in a lighter “silver heather” colorway on the Champion site for just $37 here. Choose from sizes small to 2XL. Champion says V was a perfect fit for the new campaign, citing his “unmistakable style, artistic vision and global reach” in a press release. And while he’s best known as a singer, the brand says his influence “extends beyond music, leaving an indelible mark across fashion, art and popular culture while connecting with millions of fans worldwide.” “True Champion represents a new chapter for Champion and the values that continue to define our brand,” says Stefani Fleurant, executive vice president, Marketing, Sport & Lifestyle at Authentic. “V’s creative vision, global influence and genuine connection with his audience make him a natural partner for Champion.” V joins fellow musicians Sofi Tukker, model Romeo Beckham, basketball star Kyle Kuzma, and U.S. women’s hockey player Megan Keller in the new campaign, among others. title: DOWN Announce New Album, 'Volume V' - Knotfest
content: The NOLA sludge pillars mark their mighty return with the reveal of the lead single, "Blood Oath" The powerhouse collective of  Philip H. Anselmo, Pepper Keenan, Kirk Windstein, Jimmy Bower, and Pat Bruders has confirmed their return. Sludge titans DOWN will release Volume V, the band's long-awaited LP on November 20th via Nuclear Blast Records. Decamped to Anselmo's home studio in Louisiana, the tandem of Windstein and Keenan began to build the foundation of what would be the next iteration of DOWN. Along with a pair of writing sessions, the songs that would eventually become Volume V took shape in 2025. Anselmo spoke about the next chapter of the storied brotherhood in DOWN. “We were all excited about this. There was a sense of lightness in the air. Everyone’s attitude was positive. There was more focus than ever. It just felt fresh again. Each one of us was individually striving for something, and I believe we achieved what we wanted to achieve. The record is a journey. It’s classic DOWN, but it’s also unique.”Kirk Windstein chimed in regarding the consistent creative chemistry of the band more than three decades in. “Everybody played their asses off, wrote great riffs, and Philip is singing amazing. There’s so much electricity when we get together. To me, it’s the same vibe as our debut NOLA, but we’ve got another 35 years of experience as songwriters.”Pepper Keenan added how the diversity of the individual members gels collectively. “The five of us are from the same era, grew up together, and accomplished a lot on our own. We all sounded different, but we’re still from the same 20-block radius. As far as what makes DOWN special, we knew one another before any of us had done anything. There’s history.” Volume V was produced by Eddie Mapp along with DOWN. The album also boasts a special guest appearance from the iconic King Diamond on the song, "Merciful Fate," as well as an assist from King's wife, Livia Zita. To introduce the current chapter of DOWN, the band have shared the corrosive lead single, "Blood Oath". Undeniably heavy, masterfully constructed and durable as all hell, the single offers a stylistic tip of the hat to NOLA and the timeless sludge styling that has defined DOWN for decades. “Anybody who’s from New Orleans is going to get a kick out of the references to the city,” grins Anselmo. “Musically, it’s got a big hook. It’s a DOWN song, but it takes a turn.”“You’ll know it’s DOWN right off the fucking bat,” adds Keenan. “It’s heavy in its attack.” DOWN are currently leading the charge on their North American headlining tour with  Helmet and Spirit In The Room on The Strap It Down tour. title: LDPlayer 14 Setup: 12 Steps, Hyper-V Fix [2026] - tech-insider.org
content: LDPlayer 14 shipped out of beta in late June 2026 as the first mainstream Android emulator built on Android 14, and it changed the setup process enough that guides written for LDPlayer 9 no longer apply cleanly. The headline change is native Hyper-V compatibility — a real Windows requirement that used to force gamers to choose between running LDPlayer and running Docker, WSL2, or a Windows Sandbox on the same machine. That trade-off is gone. This tutorial walks through downloading LDPlayer 14, configuring it for Hyper-V systems, tuning it for FPS in demanding mobile titles, and fixing the handful of bugs that show up most often during setup. By the end you’ll have a working LDPlayer 14 instance tuned for either single-game performance or multi-instance farming, with ADB access enabled, root toggled correctly, and a troubleshooting checklist for the errors that trip up most first-time installs. Total time: roughly 60–75 minutes including a full download and first-boot Android setup. Industry insights, the latest tech news, and special interviews, all in the Tech Insider Newsletter. This is aimed at three overlapping groups: gamers moving off LDPlayer 9 because a title now requires a newer Android API level, developers who need a GPU-accelerated Android target that doesn’t conflict with WSL2 or Docker, and anyone running multiple emulator instances for testing or farming who’s been burned by LDMultiPlayer instability in earlier builds. Each of the twelve steps below is written to work standalone, so if you already have LDPlayer 14 installed and just need the Hyper-V fix or the multi-instance setup, jump straight to that step. Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. LDPlayer 9 has been the default recommendation on most emulator lists for the last two years, and it still works fine for older titles. LDPlayer 14 is a different build, not just a version bump. It runs on an Android 14 base instead of the older Android 9/12 images LDPlayer 9 shipped with, which matters because more mobile games now ship SDK requirements that assume a newer Android API level. The official LDPlayer changelog claims up to 30% higher FPS in demanding titles compared with the previous build, a vendor number worth treating as a ceiling rather than a guarantee, but it lines up with what independent write-ups have reported after testing the new renderer path. The more practical change is Hyper-V support. LDPlayer’s March 5, 2026 Hyper-V-compatible release removed the old requirement to disable Windows’ native virtualization layer just to run the emulator. If you use WSL2, Docker Desktop, or Windows Sandbox for work, this is the single biggest reason to move off LDPlayer 9. As of the August 2026 release (build 14.0.22.0), LDPlayer also ships lower idle CPU and memory usage and a set of fixes for LDMultiPlayer, the built-in multi-instance manager, according to the version history page. It’s tempting to treat the Android version an emulator ships with as a footnote, but it changes what actually runs. App developers set a target SDK level, and Google has steadily pushed the Play Store to require newer target levels for new app submissions and updates. An emulator stuck on an Android 9 or Android 12 image increasingly hits apps that either refuse to install, install but crash on specific permission requests, or silently disable features gated behind newer Android APIs, things like updated notification channels, newer camera and media APIs, or background execution limits that some anti-cheat and DRM systems check for. Running on Android 14 doesn’t just future-proof LDPlayer against apps you haven’t installed yet. It also changes behavior for apps you already use, since some publishers ship different code paths depending on the detected Android version. If you’ve noticed a mobile game behaving oddly on LDPlayer 9, missing a UI element, failing a permission check, or refusing to launch entirely, that’s frequently an Android-version mismatch rather than an emulator bug, and it’s the first thing worth ruling out before you go digging through LDPlayer’s own settings. Before downloading anything, confirm your hardware meets the minimums. LDPlayer 14 will install on weaker machines, but “installs” and “runs a modern mobile game at 60 FPS” are two different bars. If your machine sits below the recommended tier, don’t force LDPlayer 14. GameLoop and BlueStacks 5 both remain lighter options for older hardware — see our Android emulator comparison for a full breakdown of which tool fits which hardware tier. A note on the RAM figures specifically: the 2 GB minimum is a boot floor, not a usable configuration. In practice, an instance allocated 2 GB will struggle to load the Play Store, let alone run a 3D game. Treat 8 GB as the realistic floor for casual use, 16 GB as the point where a single demanding title runs smoothly, and 32 GB as the entry point for running more than two instances at once without visible stutter. If you’re on a laptop with soldered RAM below 16 GB, LDPlayer 14 will still install and run lighter apps fine, just don’t expect the 30% FPS gain LDPlayer advertises to show up on hardware below the recommended tier — that number was measured on machines that already met or exceeded the recommended spec. Go directly to the official LDPlayer downloads page and select LDPlayer 14. Avoid third-party download mirrors — Android emulators are a common bundling target for adware installers, and the official installer is the only version guaranteed to match the changelog and version history LDPlayer publishes. The installer is a single .exe roughly 500 MB in size; the full Android system image downloads separately on first launch, which is where most of that 36 GB requirement comes from. Run the installer as Administrator. Choose a custom install path on an SSD if you have more than one drive — the default path is fine functionally, but a dedicated drive noticeably improves cold boot and app install times once you’re running real games. LDPlayer will not run without hardware virtualization turned on, and this is the single most common reason first-time installs fail immediately. Check the current state before rebooting into BIOS: If it reads Disabled, reboot into BIOS/UEFI (usually Del, F2, or F10 at boot — check your motherboard manual if unsure) and enable Intel VT-x or AMD-V, sometimes labeled AMD SVM Mode. Save and exit. This is a firmware-level setting; Windows cannot toggle it from inside the OS. This is the step that didn’t exist, or existed as a dead end, on LDPlayer 9. If you have Hyper-V, WSL2, Docker Desktop, or Windows Sandbox enabled, LDPlayer 14’s Hyper-V-compatible build (shipped March 5, 2026) means you do not need to disable those features. Confirm you’re running the Hyper-V-compatible variant: If LDPlayer still throws a virtualization conflict error on first launch despite running the Hyper-V-compatible build, open LDPlayer’s settings and switch the virtualization engine from HAXM to Hyper-V manually under Settings > Advanced > Virtualization Technology. This single toggle resolves the majority of “emulator won’t start” reports tied to Hyper-V conflicts. Launch LDPlayer 14 from the desktop shortcut. First boot takes longer than subsequent launches since Android is initializing its full system image — expect 60–90 seconds rather than the sub-10-second cold starts you’ll see afterward. Once the home screen loads, sign in with a Google account through Play Store just as you would on a physical Android 14 device. Skip any bloatware prompts LDPlayer bundles by default during first setup; they aren’t required for the emulator to function. Open the settings gear inside LDPlayer (not Windows) and go to the Performance tab. Three settings matter most: Under Resolution, match your display’s native resolution and set DPI to 240 for a phone-like touch scaling, or 160 for a tablet-like layout with more screen real estate per app. Some apps and automation tools require root. In LDPlayer 14, this is a single toggle: Settings > Other Settings > Root permission > ON. Reboot the instance after toggling. Leave root off by default unless a specific app requires it — rooted instances are more visible to anti-cheat and app-integrity checks, which can trigger bans in competitive mobile titles. Developers and power users automating tasks inside LDPlayer will want ADB enabled. Turn it on under Settings > Other Settings > ADB debugging, then connect from a terminal: If adb devices returns an empty list, restart the ADB server before trying again: Install games through the Play Store as normal, or drag-and-drop an APK file directly onto the LDPlayer window to sideload it. For games with anti-cheat systems that specifically block emulators, check the publisher’s stance first — some competitive titles ban emulator play outright, and LDPlayer cannot bypass server-side detection. For everything else, gacha games, strategy titles, and casual mobile games in particular, installation and controls work the same as BlueStacks or GameLoop. Open the Keyboard Mapping icon on the right sidebar while a game is running. LDPlayer auto-generates a default control scheme for popular titles; for less common games, build a custom map by dragging control points onto matching on-screen buttons. Save the profile per-app so it loads automatically the next time you launch that game. LDMultiPlayer, LDPlayer’s built-in multi-instance manager, received targeted bug fixes in the August 2026 release (build 14.0.22.0), making this a good time to set up multiple instances if you were previously avoiding it due to stability issues. Open the LDMultiPlayer panel from the main LDPlayer window and click “New” to spin up an additional instance. Each instance behaves as an independent device with its own IP-like ADB port (5555, 5557, 5559, and so on for each additional instance). Running more than two or three instances simultaneously is where the 32 GB RAM recommendation earns its keep. Each active instance with a 3D game loaded typically consumes 2–4 GB of RAM plus a meaningful GPU and CPU share, so budget accordingly before scaling up. To chase the vendor-claimed FPS improvements in demanding titles, layer these changes on top of the base settings from Step 5: Before making further changes, back up your configured instance. LDPlayer includes a built-in backup tool under Settings > Backup and Restore, which exports app data and settings to a single file you can restore after a reinstall or on a second machine. This step matters more with LDPlayer 14 than it did with older builds, since it’s a newer release and more likely to receive updates that occasionally require a fresh instance. An Android emulator running on your PC has the same permission model as a phone, and the same blind spots if you don’t review it. After first boot, open Settings > Apps inside the LDPlayer instance and check which apps were granted permissions automatically during install — some bundled utilities request location, storage, or contacts access by default that you don’t need for gaming. Revoke anything that isn’t tied to a game or tool you actively use. If you enabled root access in Step 6, treat that instance as higher-risk than a non-rooted one. Root removes the sandboxing that normally isolates one app’s data from another, which matters if you’re sideloading APKs from outside the Play Store. Only sideload APKs from developers or sources you trust, and consider keeping a separate, non-rooted LDPlayer instance specifically for anything you install outside the Play Store. Finally, if you’re running LDPlayer on a shared or work machine, remember that ADB debugging (Step 7) leaves a network-accessible port open on localhost by default; disable it under Settings when you’re not actively using it for automation or development work. LDPlayer’s own changelog cites up to 30% higher FPS in demanding titles when comparing LDPlayer 14 against the previous mainline build, but that’s a vendor ceiling, not an average across every game and every PC. The gain shows up most clearly in GPU-bound 3D titles running on hardware that meets or exceeds the recommended spec (Core i5-10500 / GTX 1660 Ti or better); it’s far less noticeable in 2D or lightly rendered apps, where the bottleneck was never GPU throughput to begin with. The table below breaks down where to expect the difference. The practical takeaway: if you’re chasing the headline FPS number, make sure your bottleneck is actually GPU rendering before you spend time tuning LDPlayer’s graphics settings. Running a CPU-bound strategy title and expecting a 30% jump from a renderer change will be a wasted afternoon; the fix there is core allocation and background process cleanup, not the DirectX/OpenGL toggle. If an instance gets into a state you can’t troubleshoot out of, a clean reset is often faster than debugging further. LDPlayer separates a full uninstall from a per-instance reset, and it’s worth knowing the difference before you reach for either. Before wiping an instance, remember the backup step from Step 12 — a saved backup file lets you restore app data and keymaps to a freshly reset or reinstalled instance instead of reconfiguring everything from scratch. Most of these aren’t unique to LDPlayer specifically, they show up across every major Android-on-PC emulator, but the specific fixes above are tuned to how LDPlayer 14’s settings menu is laid out, which differs enough from LDPlayer 9’s layout that muscle memory from the old version will occasionally send you to the wrong menu during your first few sessions. If you hit an error not covered above, isolate whether it’s an LDPlayer issue or a Windows/GPU driver issue before spending time in LDPlayer’s own settings. A quick way to check: if other virtualization-dependent software (Docker Desktop, WSL2, Android Studio’s own emulator) is also failing on the same machine, the problem is almost certainly at the Windows or BIOS level, not inside LDPlayer 14 specifically. Fix that layer first, then retest LDPlayer. Everything above works as standalone reference, but if you’re setting up a machine from scratch, it helps to have the whole sequence in one place. This is the exact order to run through for a clean install that ends with a tuned, backed-up, ADB-accessible LDPlayer 14 instance. Running through this list top to bottom on a fresh Windows 11 install with a GTX 1660 Ti-class GPU should land you at a working, tuned instance in well under the 60–75 minute estimate given at the top of this guide, most of that time is the initial download and first Android boot, not the configuration itself. Once the base setup is stable, a few advanced adjustments squeeze out more performance or convenience. First, if you’re running LDMultiPlayer across many instances, stagger their launches instead of starting them all simultaneously — each cold boot is CPU-intensive, and launching ten instances at once will bottleneck every one of them during the boot window. Second, for automation workflows, LDPlayer’s Android Debug Bridge access can be scripted the same way as a physical device or Android Studio’s own emulator, which makes LDPlayer a viable, GPU-accelerated alternative to the stock Android Studio AVD for teams doing UI testing on a budget. Third, if you split time between LDPlayer and other Android emulators for compatibility testing across different Android versions, keep LDPlayer 9 installed in parallel for apps that specifically target older API levels, rather than trying to force backward compatibility inside a single Android 14 instance. Finally, for anyone doing sustained multi-instance farming, a dedicated SSD scratch partition for LDPlayer’s instance data noticeably reduces I/O contention versus sharing a drive with the OS and other applications. LDPlayer 14 isn’t the only serious option for Android gaming on PC in 2026, and it isn’t automatically the right one for every setup. If your machine sits closer to the minimum spec tier, or you specifically need a lighter footprint, GameLoop remains a solid pick for lower-end hardware — see our GameLoop emulator setup guide. BlueStacks 5 is still the most broadly compatible option for casual and social-gaming apps, and our BlueStacks 5 setup guide covers its own install path in detail. For a full side-by-side across FPS, RAM footprint, and stability, our Android emulator for PC comparison breaks all three down against MuMu Player and others in one table. Beyond gaming, LDPlayer 14 has become a practical stand-in for developers who need a fast, GPU-accelerated Android target without pulling the full weight of Android Studio’s own AVD manager onto a machine. It won’t replace a proper CI-driven test matrix across real devices, but for local UI iteration, checking a layout against Android 14’s newer permission dialogs, or scripting basic interactions with ADB, it starts faster than a cold Android Studio emulator and doesn’t compete with Android Studio’s own virtualization stack the way older LDPlayer builds did before Hyper-V support landed. If you’re already using Android Studio’s official emulator for CI or automated testing, keep that as the source of truth for release validation. LDPlayer 14’s value here is speed during day-to-day local development, not as a replacement for Google’s own tooling on anything that touches a release pipeline. For most users still on LDPlayer 9, the honest answer is: yes, if you use Hyper-V, WSL2, or Docker Desktop regularly, and yes if you play titles that specifically require an Android 14-level API. If neither applies and your current LDPlayer 9 setup is stable, there’s no urgent reason to migrate mid-season — LDPlayer 9 continues to function and receives maintenance updates. The clearer signal to move is the August 2026 LDMultiPlayer stability patch; if multi-instance crashes have been a persistent annoyance, that fix alone often justifies the switch. Yes. LDPlayer 14, like previous LDPlayer versions, is free to download and use, with no paywall on core features like multi-instance mode or keyboard mapping. The developer generates revenue through optional ad placements inside the launcher and partnerships rather than a license fee, so you shouldn’t hit a paywall during setup or normal use. No. LDPlayer is Windows-only, and that hasn’t changed with the LDPlayer 14 release. Mac users typically look at alternatives built for macOS specifically, since LDPlayer’s virtualization layer relies on Windows-native technologies like Hyper-V and HAXM that don’t have a macOS equivalent in this emulator’s architecture. Yes, they can coexist as separate installations. This is useful if some of your apps or games are better tested against an older Android base while you migrate the rest of your library to LDPlayer 14. Most of that footprint is the Android 14 system image plus space reserved for app installs and instance data. It’s a listed minimum on the official version history page, not a hard cap — heavier game libraries or multiple instances will use considerably more. LDPlayer itself, downloaded from the official ldplayer.net site, is a legitimate and widely used emulator. Risk comes primarily from third-party download mirrors that bundle adware installers, which is why this guide points exclusively to the official download page. It depends on the game’s anti-cheat policy. Competitive titles with strict app-integrity checks are more likely to flag rooted emulator instances. Leave root disabled unless a specific app you use requires it. There’s no hard software limit built into LDPlayer itself, but practical limits come from RAM and GPU capacity. Each active 3D-game instance typically uses 2–4 GB of RAM plus a meaningful GPU share, so a 32 GB system comfortably supports several instances before performance degrades, while an 8–16 GB system is better suited to one or two instances at a time. Both are virtualization engines LDPlayer can use to run the Android system. HAXM was the traditional default and conflicts with Windows’ native Hyper-V feature, forcing a choice between the emulator and tools like WSL2. LDPlayer 14’s Hyper-V mode lets the emulator run through Windows’ built-in virtualization layer instead, which is what allows it to coexist with WSL2, Docker Desktop, and Windows Sandbox without disabling any of them first. Most apps and games install and run fine through the Play Store inside LDPlayer 14, but Play Protect certification issues occasionally surface after a fresh install or a major LDPlayer update, showing up as a sign-in or certification error. Clearing the Play Store’s app data and re-signing in inside the instance resolves this in most cases, as noted in the troubleshooting table above. If LDPlayer 9 is stable for the games you play and you don’t need Hyper-V compatibility, there’s no urgent reason to switch immediately. The clearest signals to move are needing Hyper-V/WSL2 coexistence, wanting the patched LDMultiPlayer for multi-instance stability, or hitting compatibility issues tied to an older Android base on newer game releases. title: The 2027 Hyundai Tucson's Radical Redesign Puts Real Pressure On The RAV4 And CR-V - Top Speed
content: Hyundai revealed the fifth-generation Tucson today, and it looks nothing like the compact SUV segment has seen before. Gone is the soft, rounded body of the outgoing model. In its place: a boxy, angular silhouette with prominent fender flares, full-width LED light bars front and rear, and vertical daytime running lights — a design Hyundai calls "Art of Steel." It's a sharp departure, and it's clearly aimed at shaking up a segment that has long rewarded playing it safe. The timing matters. The Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V have dominated compact SUV sales for years by offering incremental updates and proven reliability rather than bold styling. With this fifth-generation Tucson — larger, more tech-forward, and dramatically more aggressive-looking than its predecessor — Hyundai is betting that buyers are ready for something different. The numbers tell part of the story. The 2027 Tucson grows 2.3 inches (60 mm) in overall length to 185 inches (4,700 mm), and stretches 1.57 inches (40 mm) wider to 75 inches (1,905 mm). The wheelbase extends 1.1 inches (30 mm) to 109.6 inches (2,785 mm), and overall height rises 0.8 inches (20 mm) to 66.3 inches (1,685 mm). That extra height translates directly into 1.1 inches (29 mm) more rear-seat headroom — a meaningful gain for a family hauler. Beyond the dimensions, the design itself is the statement. The squared-off quarter panels, sharp body lines across the door skins, and beefy rocker panels give the Tucson a planted, almost architectural stance. Both ends feature an illuminated H motif that makes the headlights and taillights look nearly interchangeable — a deliberate, space-age symmetry. Rear door opening angle increases from 73 to 83 degrees, a practical touch that makes loading kids and cargo noticeably easier. Hyundai's design chief SangYup Lee has framed the boxy direction across the Santa Fe and Palisade as a move to strengthen outdoor-lifestyle appeal, and the Tucson carries that logic into the heart of the compact segment. Inside, the 2027 Tucson adopts Hyundai's new Pleos infotainment system, centered on a large touchscreen — likely in the range of 17 inches based on its use in the Grandeur, though Hyundai hasn't confirmed the exact size for this application. A slim digital instrument display sits high on the dashboard, positioned above the steering wheel's upper rim in a way that mimics a head-up display. Physical controls remain underneath the main screen, which is a welcome concession to usability. The cabin's character is defined by a rounded center console, a two-spoke steering wheel, orange dashboard accents, perforated upholstery, wood trim, and ambient lighting. Dual wireless smartphone charging pads are confirmed. The overall effect reads less like a mainstream compact crossover and more like something from a segment above — which is precisely the competitive ground Hyundai is trying to claim against the CR-V's polished but conventional interior and the RAV4's rugged-but-functional cabin. Hyundai has not released any powertrain specifications with this design reveal. What the sources confirm is the expectation of both hybrid and non-hybrid versions, consistent with the current Tucson's lineup structure. The existing model offers a 2.5-liter naturally aspirated four-cylinder as the base engine, a turbocharged 1.6-liter four-cylinder paired with an electric motor for the hybrid, and a plug-in hybrid version of that same 1.6-liter turbo with a larger battery. The next-generation model is expected to carry forward this general architecture, likely updated for improved efficiency. A rugged XRT trim has already been previewed, featuring a distinct front grille with a rectangular motif, contrast black wheel arches, skid plate inserts, and touch-sensitive LED taillighting. Hyundai plans a Korean launch later this year, with broader global availability expected in 2027. The compact SUV segment is one of the most competitive in the industry, and the RAV4 and CR-V have historically won it on reliability reputation and steady refinement rather than design risk. The RAV4 leans into its rugged aesthetic with squared-off body cladding and trail-ready trim levels like the TRD Off-Road and Trail. The CR-V takes the opposite approach — clean, restrained, and interior-focused. Neither has made a styling leap as dramatic as what Hyundai is attempting here. Hyundai moved 234,000 Tucsons in the U.S. last year, making it the brand's top-selling vehicle by a significant margin — 86,000 units ahead of the second-place Elantra. That volume gives Hyundai something real to protect, which is why the powertrain strategy is expected to stay conservative even as the design goes bold. The new Tucson's size increase also positions it more squarely against the RAV4 and CR-V on interior space, an area where both competitors have traditionally held an edge. Whether buyers respond to the styling gamble or retreat to the familiar will be the real test when the Tucson reaches showrooms. We want to hear from you. title: Recapping Travis Hunter's day, snap counts in joint practice v. Panthers - Jaguars Wire
content: With the Jacksonville Jaguars hosting the Carolina Panthers on Wednesday for a joint practice, let's take a look at where Travis Hunter lined up and how he performed. During the previous two days, almost every one of Hunter's 11-on-11 snaps came at cornerback. That continued in the joint practice. ESPN's Michael DiRocco was tracking each one of Hunter's team reps and noted that he played 30 total snaps, with 28 of them coming on offense. DiRocco noted that Hunter had two standout plays on defense, forcing a pass breakup on one attempt and then a throwaway on another while defending Panthers' wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan. Jamal St. Cyr also posted that Hunter came up to make a stop on a short throw from Panthers' quarterback Bryce Young to running back Jonathon Brooks. Hunter's heavy usage on defense seems to be the new norm -- at least for the time being. As was the expectation coming into training camp, Hunter is going to play a key role at cornerback this season, with the Jaguars still wanting to get him involved on offense as well, although what his playing time looks like at wide receiver isn't as obvious and could ebb and flow from week to week. In total this summer, Hunter has played 229 snaps in 11-on-11 with 163 coming on defense and 65 on offense.

title: Star Trek Follows Gen V & Evil Dead With Its Wildest Twist Yet - Yahoo
content: The Star Trek franchise is following in the footsteps of Gen V and Evil Dead. Their new episodes have come in with the wildest twist yet in the series' decades-long history. According to a recent report from CinemaBlend, Star Trek: Strange New Worlds is officially delivering a puppet episode for fans. The entire crew will transform into puppets following a 'Level-Five Transporter Incident.' Thankfully, going by the pictures shared by the website's newsletter, Captain Spock does not appear to be affected by the transformation, as he maintains his original form. The synopsis reads, per TrekMovie, "A transporter malfunction turns most of the crew into puppets while Spock fights to reclaim the ship." Now then, this particular episode is enough evidence that the franchise is trying to mimic the Evil Dead and the Gen V franchise. For context, both franchises had puppet scenes or episodes that garnered significant reactions from the fans. Strange New Worlds has been quite brave in its approach to the Star Trek stories. Throughout the season, there have been new experiments that surprised the fans. For example, the fourth episode, which is titled A Case of Chiaroscuro, has reportedly adapted the old Hollywood noir movies and will drop in black-and-white. A similar sort of experimentation was done when the director dropped a horror-themed episode. Titled The Griffin Incident, the episode tried to direct the Star Trek story into a spooky world. Directed by Axelle Carolyn, the director told TrekMovie in an interview, "I understand the criticism about the answers not being given at the end, like the scientific explanation… That was also something we discussed, and I felt like I understand that one of the tenets of Star Trek is we can explore the universe, and science would always bring us home and help us understand what's going on." Despite occasional backlash, Strange New Worlds continues to prove that it isn't afraid to experiment with new formats while keeping the core spirit of exploration alive. title: AMD's Zen 7 architecture will offer 512 MB of 3D V-Cache and 32 compute cores. - GameGPU
content: AMD is formulating a long-term platform development strategy for several processor generations ahead. With the Zen 6 generation, the manufacturer will address the limitations of the Zen 5 architecture by implementing a redesigned memory controller, new low-latency interconnect dies, and increased core counts. The next lineup, based on the Zen 7 architecture, will transition to the advanced A14 process technology, offering configurations with up to 32 cores and a massive 3D V-Cache stack with a capacity of up to 16 MB per core, providing flagship chips with a total cache of up to 512 MB at clock speeds up to 7.2 GHz. Such a significant performance boost within the AM5 socket raises the question of whether users will need to upgrade to the AM6 socket with the Zen 8 architecture in the future. While Zen 6 and Zen 7 will be sufficient for typical gaming tasks for many years to come, the advancement of the AM6 platform will rely on changing workloads. The architecture of future solutions is optimized for autonomous AI agents and local computing, where aggregate bandwidth, cache capacity, and support for the new DDR6 memory standard are critical. Local AI algorithms are gradually moving beyond data centers and discrete NPUs. The core architecture of Zen 7 and Zen 8 processors is designed to directly execute complex neural network chains using the CPU in conjunction with accelerators. The high price of the new platform's components, including $500–$600 motherboards and new memory modules, will target users building high-performance local workstations for next-generation complex tasks. title: Down Announce New Album Volume V, Unleash “Blood Oath”: Stream - Consequence of Sound
content:
Log in to track artists, discover shows, and stay in the loop. Volume V will arrive November 20th via Nuclear Blast Records Down have announced their new album, Volume V, set to arrive November 20th via Nuclear Blast Records. Ahead of its release, the band has unleashed lead single “Blood Oath.” “Blood Oath” is a nasty doom grinder, as Philip Anselmo’s vocals evoke Matt Pike of High on Fire with the heft of the partial growl set against a riff that is pure New Orleans sludge metal. The influence of classic doom from Trouble and St. Vitus is worn plain as day by the riffs that make up “Blood Oath,” underscoring why Down has been able to sustain such profound critical and commercial interest despite having released just three LPs and two EPs over their 35-year history. Anselmo stated of the new album, “We were all excited about this. There was a sense of lightness in the air. Everyone’s attitude was positive. There was more focus than ever. It just felt fresh again. Each one of us was individually striving for something, and I believe we achieved what we wanted to achieve. The record is a journey. It’s classic Down, but it’s also unique.” Founding guitarist Kirk Weinstein, who returned to the fold for this album following his absence on Down Volume 4 – Part II, added, “Everybody played their asses off, wrote great riffs, and Philip is singing amazing. There’s so much electricity when we get together. To me, it’s the same vibe as our debut NOLA, but we’ve got another 35 years of experience as songwriters.” The album also features the song “Merciful Fate,” an ode to Mercyful Fate that features King Diamond and his wife Livia Zita, as well as a song titled “Ozz” in honor of Ozzy Osbourne. Down are currently on tour in North America alongside Helmet and Spirit in the Room, and will also  perform at Zakk Wylde’s upcoming Berzerkus festival. Get tickets here. title: 10 V-Twins That Deliver More Than Just Nostalgia - Top Speed
content: Nostalgia is an integral element for most V-twin motorcycles today. It works in favor of brands like Harley-Davidson and Indian, both of which enjoy a rich history as the forefathers of the V-twin engine. However, in these modern times, all bikemakers have realized nostalgia alone isn’t enough. There needs to be more, which has birthed some interesting V-twin machines in recent times. We’ve jotted down 10 such motorcycles, all of which justify the nostalgia aspect while packing something extra. Most of these are available new today, but some of them aren’t. For the longest time, Ducati stuck to the adventure-touring world with its Multistrada range. But when the popularity of hardcore ADVs picked up, the brand stepped up its game with the DesertX. Since its debut, one of the bike’s highlights has been its nostalgic design that pays homage to the iconic Cagiva Elefante dakar bike. Dual headlights, white paint, a flat seat, and a sleek tail all prove that well. Look past the retro charm, though, and you find a hardcore ADV capable of doing some serious off-roading. This is thanks to the inclusion of high-end suspension from KYB with nearly 9 inches of travel at both ends and 21/18-inch spoke wheels. Those things also equate to a ground clearance of nearly 10 inches of ground clearance. A couple of decades ago, Ducati created the Monster as a parts bin special. Little did the brand know it’d become a lifesaver. Accordingly, the naked bike has been on sale since, with a pinch of the OG nostalgia in every version. That is true for the latest V2 as well, evident from its oval headlight, stripped-back design, minimalistic tail, and dual exhausts. Underneath, though, this is a thoroughly new machine. It features one of Ducati’s most advanced (and lightest) V-twins yet, complete with modern-day bits like intake variable valve timing, hollow valve stems, a racing-derived lubrication system, thin inner walls, and aluminum cylinder liners. Topping things off is a set of premium rider aids derived from the world of racing. What you’re looking at is the most powerful mass-market V-twin air-cooled cruiser bike on sale right now. Credit for that goes to its new Milwaukee-Eight 117 High Output engine, featuring a forward-facing Heavy Breather intake, a performance-tuned 2-into-1 exhaust, a high-performance SE8-511 camshaft, and a raised redline. Adding more modernity are dual disc brakes and a USD fork up top. Even with all that, the nostalgia remains an integral aspect. The Low Rider S takes heavy inspiration from OG FXLR Low Riders from yesteryear, evident from the stretched-out forks, minimalistic lights, and a slim overall appearance unlike other Softails. There’s even a new Chrome version now for an added retro touch. And it’s cheaper than the blacked-out trim! The CVO Street Glide Limited is Harley’s flagship full-dresser touring bike right now. It gets the nostalgia aspect right with a batwing fairing like OG Street Glides, along with an overall larger-than-life aesthetic like previous ‘Limited’ models. Look past the nostalgia, though, and you’ll notice the Street Glide spoils you with several technological advancements. The engine is where it starts. This has the top-drawer Milwaukee-Eight 121 powerhouse, producing 115 horsepower and 139 pound-feet. The party trick here is the VVT system, which spreads the power across the rev range. Then, you have the endless luxury. Right from the chrome floorboards and grips to the heated seats and chrome wheels, every element is flagship here. Rockford Fosgate speakers are standard, too. The Sportster S takes design inspiration from Harley-Davidson’s iconic flat-track-dominating machines. The swept-up exhaust, minimalistic fenders, and an angular tank are all reminiscent of the retro flat trackers, while the chunky wheels serve as an homage to the old Forty-Eight. The nostalgia is further amplified with the ‘Blood Orange’ colorway, inspired straight from the XR750. Besides the nostalgia, you get one of the most advanced cruiser bikes from an American bikemaker. Not only do you get modern equipment as standard (adjustable USD forks with an aluminum triple clamp and six-axis IMU-enabled electronics), but the engine itself is a work of art. The 1,252cc Revolution Max V-twin has full liquid cooling, variable valve timing, dual-downdraft throttle bodies, internal balancers, and forged pistons–all of which are rarities in the American cruiser market. The Pursuit is Indian’s flagship full dresser (until a new Elite comes along). It follows the norm of a traditional American touring bike with a large fairing, saddlebags, and a top box. But it tops that off with some never-before-seen bits in the American-made touring segment. The presence of a rear radar is arguably the biggest deal here, which enables collision detection and blind spot monitoring. These can be life-savers on massive American freeways. In addition, the rear end has electronic preload settings. This helps boost stability with varying loads with a click of a button (rider only, rider and luggage, rider and pillion, or rider, pillion, and luggage). Finally, there’s the fully liquid-cooled V-twin powerhouse that is smaller in size than the CVO’s V-twin but produces around 10 more horsepower. The Road Glide moniker has always been about comfort and usable performance, packaged in an old-school bagger look. But a couple of years ago, Harley woke up and chose violence to give us the CVO Road Glide ST. While this still had all the nostalgic elements like a sharknose fairing and massive saddlebags, the ST in its name brought heavy influence from the King Of The Bagger class. Accordingly, the engine here has high-performance internals and a Screamin’ Eagle exhaust to produce 127 horsepower–the highest for any Road Glide (barring the $100,000 RR). This is topped with adjustable USD forks and rear shocks, petal rotors with Brembo monoblocs, and lightweight aluminum wheels. You also get a helping of forged carbon parts for the first time! Arch Motorcycles is a luxury bikemaker that builds non-mass-production bikes well beyond the reach of regular customers. So budget is not a constraint, meaning there’s no shortage of high-end equipment, be it the Ohlins suspension, billet aluminum chassis elements, or an S&S powerhouse. The KRGT-1 has all of that, while featuring old-school cruiser elements for a kick of nostalgia. A round headlight sits up top, flanked by raked-out forks and a 19-inch front wheel. This is topped with a low-slung saddle and forward-set footpegs to create a laid-back riding triangle. The tank and tail follow the retro theme, too, with indents for the former and a curvy arch for the latter. From afar, the Super Cruiser looks like any other regular cruiser. It is low and long, topped with round lights and a teardrop-shaped fuel tank. Plus, the handlebar sits on tall risers, and the saddle is shaped like an old-school chopper for an upright riding triangle. But the closer you look, the more it surprises you. The biggest surprise is the V-twin engine. This comes from a sports bike and only has a mild detune, promising an impressive 175 horsepower. The underpinnings follow the same brief, featuring Fox suspension, 17-inch wheels, and dual 320 mm petal discs that mimic sports bikes. All of that, along with the high-set pegs, gives the Super Cruiser a cornering clearance of 50 degrees on each side–15 more than the Sportster S above. Not long ago, Indian pulled the plug on the FTR. But if you want an American roadster with nostalgia and something extra, this still ranks high up the recommendation list. Its exclusivity is a big reason, considering we haven’t had any actual old-school flat-track-inspired roadster from America in several years. What adds to this is the brilliant package. The V-twin engine has immense power and torque for serious regular riding fun, the trellis chassis means a sub-520-pound weight, and the adjustable suspension is properly sporty with 17-inch wheels. You can also transform this into a proper track tool or actual flat-tracker, as Indian used to race the FTR in both categories not long ago. We want to hear from you.
